contributions: An elastic token budget training framework for visual object tracking, so that one trained tracker operates across varying computational budgets rather than the fixed budget it was pruned for.

A result-driven token importance criterion, in which a policy network estimating token importance is optimized under the supervision of the tracker's localization precision, aligning importance estimation with tracking accuracy.
A budget-collaborative optimization strategy that trains the tracker across multiple budgets jointly, alternating with the importance-estimation step.
limitations: The abstract available for this record reports no numbers, names no benchmark and no baseline tracker, so nothing can be said here about the accuracy cost of elasticity — in particular whether a single elastic tracker matches a tracker trained for each fixed budget, which is the comparison the claim depends on. No stated limitations section is available. The available material also does not state the range of budgets covered, the granularity at which the budget can be set at inference, or the runtime overhead of the policy network itself. This record was written from the ICML 2026 abstract only; no preprint or full text was locatable.
method: ETBTrack is an elastic token budget training framework for visual trackers. It has two parts. First, a result-driven importance criterion: rather than scoring image tokens by a hand-designed proxy, a policy network estimates token importance and is optimized under the supervision of the tracker's localization precision, so that the importance estimator and the tracking objective are aligned on the same quantity. Second, a budget-collaborative optimization strategy: the tracker is optimized jointly across several token budgets instead of one, so a single set of weights is compatible with a range of them. The two optimization processes — the policy network for importance and the tracker across budgets — are run alternately, which is what produces the elastic inference behaviour.
one_liner: ETBTrack trains a single visual object tracker to run under a range of image-token pruning budgets, using a policy network supervised by localization precision to rank token importance and an alternating optimization that exposes the tracker to varying budgets.
problem: Visual tracking estimates a target's state across a video, and deployments differ widely in the compute they can spend. Existing efficient trackers prune image tokens against a fixed budget chosen at training time, so a trained tracker is locked to that one operating point and cannot adapt to the range of compute available in real deployments. Retraining one model per budget is the alternative the paper is arguing against.

relevance.overthinking: This is a keyword false positive and should be recorded as one. The task matched on 'token budget', but the tokens are image patch tokens inside a vision transformer tracker and the budget is a FLOP/latency budget for pruning them; there is no language model, no chain of thought, and no reasoning length. Nothing here concerns how long a model deliberates, when it should stop, or the accuracy/efficiency tradeoff of test-time reasoning — the tracker's compute is spent on perceiving a frame, not on thinking about a problem. The only structural echo of the topic is at the level of analogy: one model trained to operate at several compute budgets rather than one, with importance scored against the end task rather than a proxy. That analogy is worth at most a sentence if the group ever writes about elastic reasoning-length models; it is not evidence for anything in this topic, and the paper should not be counted toward any concept's evidence for overthinking. Recommend dropping from the topic, and treating 'token budget' as a keyword that needs a reasoning-context qualifier.
